scope: Written audit of the actual zero-denominator Schur boundary. It is not a new input family, universal harmonic proof, independent review or parent adoption.
finding: At a polygon equality a_bar(i)=s-2p_i=0 with 0<s<1, the affected zero-supported weight-three directions contribute exact zero eigenvalues to M(sigma)-I, and the 1111 pivot is strictly negative. If the remaining harmonic inequality W<=1 holds, the actual second-smallest eigenvalue is exactly 1 and lambda_2(H1(rho)+tilde(rho)) is exactly 3. A zero denominator alone does not establish W<=1.
written_derivation: From the actual Schmidt/union inequality, 0=s-2p_i >= E[(N_bar_i-1)_+] >= 2(P_bar(i)+P_1111), so both probabilities vanish. Any other positive-sector zero denominator arises from another saturated site and also has zero amplitude. In M(sigma)-I=H1(sigma)-I-sigma, each such zero computational vector is therefore a zero eigenvector and has no row/column coupling. The 1111 diagonal pivot is -(1-s) <0 because q4=0. As in 121's exact Schur complement, the condition for the remaining positive-sector block to be PSD is W<=1, where W omits all true zero denominators. The zero eigenvector makes the second-smallest eigenvalue at most 1; PSD of the remaining block makes it at least 1. No assumption is made that every boundary state can be approximated by states satisfying the harmonic inequality.
continuity_qualification: The ordered eigenvalues of H1(rho)+tilde(rho) are continuous functions of rho (Weyl/Lipschitz), while 140 gives an explicit actual pure-state path on which the auxiliary W jumps by 1/3. These statements are compatible: W is not itself an invariant eigenvalue and no W-continuity or 0/0 limiting cancellation is allowed.
logical_boundary: A zero-supported direction and a negative pivot alone do NOT rule out another negative Schur eigenvalue. General W<=1 remains open. If W>1 at such a point, the second-smallest eigenvalue is below 1 despite an additional zero, and the actual strengthened spectral condition fails. This note does not assert that such a physical point exists.
